abstract: The relationship between brain lesions and cognition is enigmatic. Apparently similar lesions can produce different outcomes. Stroke provides a prototypical model to understand how lesion anatomy, network disruption, prior injury and patient characteristics shape impairment. We analysed 3,034 patients from 13 acute ischaemic stroke cohorts, integrating infarct size and location, structural and functional lesion network mapping, pre-existing cerebrovascular injury, and demographic and clinical characteristics to predict impairment across six cognitive domains within one year after stroke. Infarct topography and connectivity improved prediction for six of seven outcomes over demographic, clinical and infarct-size information alone. Structural lesion connectivity accounted for most gains, with additional gains from topography and connectivity of pre-existing vascular lesions. Across domains, gains rested on left anterior thalamic connectivity plus domain-specific anatomy. Our findings establish, at unprecedented scale, that understanding lesion-cognition relationships requires looking beyond the lesion to networks, prior brain pathology and individual context.
authors: Schaper, F. L. W. V. J.
